title: Given an array of elements and a value K, return the K most frequent elements, in any order.
shortTitle: Top K Frequent Elements — HashMap frequency + min-heap or bucket sort

s1_definition.profdef: Count each element's frequency in a HashMap, then select the top K either with a size-K min-heap ordered by frequency, giving n log K time, or with bucket sort where buckets are indexed by frequency, giving linear time. The bucket approach exploits that frequencies range only from one to n.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of finding the three most common transaction types in a day. First you tally how many times each type occurred. Then either you keep a shortlist of the three highest tallies, swapping out the smallest whenever a higher one appears, or you drop each type into a bucket labelled by its count and read the buckets from the high-count end until you have three.
s1_definition.oneliner: Tally frequencies in a HashMap, then take the top K with a size-K min-heap (O(n log K)) or with frequency-indexed bucket sort (O(n)).
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Count each element's frequency in a HashMap, then select the top K either with a size-K min-heap ordered by frequency, giving n log K time, or with bucket sort where buckets are indexed by frequency, giving linear time. The bucket approach exploits that frequencies range only from one to n.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of finding the three most common transaction types in a day. First you tally how many times each type occurred. Then either you keep a shortlist of the three highest tallies, swapping out the smallest whenever a higher one appears, or you drop each type into a bucket labelled by its count and read the buckets from the high-count end until you have three.

**One line to remember:** Tally frequencies in a HashMap, then take the top K with a size-K min-heap (O(n log K)) or with frequency-indexed bucket sort (O(n)).

sections.s2_technical:
First build a frequency map from element to its count in one pass. For example: `freq.merge(x, 1, Integer::sum);`. This costs linear time and holds one entry per distinct element.

The heap approach maintains a min-heap of size K ordered by frequency. It offers each distinct element and, when the heap exceeds K, removes the least frequent, so the K most frequent remain. For example: `heap.offer(entry); if (heap.size() > K) heap.poll();` with a comparator on count. This costs n log K.

The bucket approach creates an array of buckets indexed from zero to n, placing each element into the bucket equal to its frequency, then scans buckets from the highest index downward collecting elements until K are gathered. For example: `buckets[freq.get(x)].add(x);` then iterate from the top. Because a frequency can be at most n, the bucket array is bounded and the whole method is linear.

A senior nuance is choosing bucket sort when K is large or linear time matters, since it beats the heap's log factor, while the heap is preferable when K is small relative to the number of distinct elements or when memory for n buckets is undesirable. Both begin with the same frequency map; they differ only in the selection step.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, the operations dashboard shows the K most frequent transaction types for the day. The system must count occurrences and return the top K types. This is exactly how Top K Frequent works — frequency counting followed by top-K selection.

Problem 2 — The daily volume is large and the dashboard must refresh quickly, so a linear selection is attractive. This is exactly why bucket sort is used, with the min-heap noted as the alternative for small K.

The mini-project builds a `TopKFrequentService` with both methods, a `BankLogFormatter`, and a runnable demo over a day's transaction-type list.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is ten transaction types and K equal to two.

Step 1: The frequency pass tallies UPI five times, NEFT twice, ATM twice, and IMPS once.

Step 2: The heap method offers each distinct type with its count into a min-heap ordered by frequency, keeping only the two most frequent. After processing, the heap holds UPI with five and one of the twos.

Step 3: Since IMPS has count one and the ATM and NEFT have two, the heap drops IMPS first and keeps UPI and whichever of ATM or NEFT it saw, both having count two.

Step 4: The bucket method builds buckets indexed by count, placing UPI in bucket five, NEFT and ATM in bucket two, IMPS in bucket one.

Step 5: It scans from the highest bucket down, collecting UPI from bucket five, then reaching bucket two and collecting one more until two items are gathered.

Step 6: Both methods return the top two, UPI being clearly first and the second being a type with count two.

```text
2026-10-26T21:00:00Z [INFO] National Bank of India — Top K Transaction Types
2026-10-26T21:00:00Z [INFO] Top 2 (heap) -> [NEFT, UPI]
2026-10-26T21:00:00Z [INFO] Top 2 (bucket) -> [UPI, ATM]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  types → frequency map:
    UPI:5  NEFT:2  ATM:2  IMPS:1

  Heap (size K=2 by freq):
    offer all → drop least → keeps {UPI:5, one-of-2}

  Bucket sort (index = frequency):
    [1]→IMPS  [2]→NEFT,ATM  [5]→UPI
    scan high→low: UPI(5), then a 2 → stop at K=2
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Top K Frequent Elements always starts with one linear pass to build a frequency map from each element to its count. The only decision is how to select the K highest counts from that map, and I know two methods.

The min-heap method keeps a heap of size K ordered by frequency: I offer each distinct element and, when the heap exceeds K, I remove the least frequent, so the K most frequent survive. This costs n log K and is best when K is small compared to the number of distinct elements. The bucket-sort method exploits the fact that a frequency can be at most n, so I create n plus one buckets indexed by frequency, drop each element into the bucket matching its count, and scan from the highest-count bucket downward collecting elements until I have K. That is linear time, with no log factor, which is why I prefer it when K is large or latency matters.

The insight interviewers reward is recognizing that frequencies are bounded by n, which is exactly what makes bucket sort linear and lets it beat the heap. Both share the identical first step and differ only in selection, so I describe the trade-off rather than treating one as universally correct.

In my project at National Bank of India, the operations dashboard displayed the K most frequent transaction types for the day. Because daily volume was large and the dashboard had to refresh quickly, I used bucket sort for linear selection, keeping the min-heap as the fallback when K was tiny relative to the handful of distinct types, so the tiles updated without a sorting bottleneck.
